doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

title: Writing while walking, copyists and the Synclavier
summary: Gold composes in his head on walks, sends work to a copyist, and still values the Synclavier over screens.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Do you find that you are working on assignments even when you're not working? You go for a walk and you've still got this —

Oh yeah yeah. Especially when over the years of my lifetime I used to do my best writing when I took my power walk in the morning. You know? I would hear the song and I'd start finishing it — I'd come home, I'd grab a piece of paper and I'd start correcting what I had in my head or where I had left it the day before. Absolutely. I never thought a song was finished until I could hear it in my head completely be it in bed in the morning or, you know, I would feel much better about my arrangement if I had it that rote in me, you know, if it was that big a part of me at that moment.
What do you send in what form is your music in when you send it to your copyist?

A couple of different ways either written, either written out on the score paper, or I've used one guy who has perfect pitch and he can take my arrangement and I separate — I do the violins on the left, the violas on the right and the cello in the middle. And you know from my Synclavier he writes out my arrangements and sends me a fair copy and then I take the fair copy and I re—work that with a pencil and I work on that for a couple of days and then I call him up on Zoom and I say here are my changes and it's done.
I think it's really cool that you — a Synclavier goes back how many years now?
And it's still useful for you.

Big time. Yeah I mean it's not state—of—the—art sound—wise at this point, you know, the way I have it. But as far as my memory and it's like a big tape recorder that I can work on parts of the song. You can do that now with computers but who wants to look at a screen all day long? I don't want to look at a screen all day long, I hate looking at the phone as much as we look at the phone these days. You know? I mean I find myself reading the paper on the phone, and then later I'll play a crossword on the phone. I mean you end up doing so much on the phone. Whereas the Synclavier, it's like a digital tape recorder. So I can spot the different spots of the song, and like I said I can sit here and listen to it. You know? I'm not saying that I don't — I have my score paper right here and a lot of times my best ideas I write at home and bring them in and then I put them in the Synclavier and listen to them. But I've grown lazy over the course of my lifetime.
